ca_high_energy_wall.blurb: High Energy Wall is a steep granite face in Cloudburst Canyon, part of the Woodfords Canyon cluster beside Highway 88 near the Carson River. It holds about twenty routes, nearly all of them trad, mostly crack lines, plus a pair of bolted sport pitches including a showy arete on the northern edge. Difficulty runs from the high 5.8s up into the low 5.13s, with the bulk in the 5.10 to 5.12 range, so it suits climbers who already lead solid trad. The wall sits a short scramble up the slope above the lower parking flats, partly screened by aspens. Expect a quiet, single-pitch day.

ca_dog_boulder.blurb: Dog Boulder is a single large granite block in the pines near Horseshoe Lake, up in the Mammoth Lakes basin at roughly 9,000 feet. It is a mellow spot for technical, balance-driven problems rather than power: the faces are not steep and the landings are flat. About twenty problems wrap around the block, from a very easy one up to a V4, with most between V0 and V2. Because climbs sit on every side, you can usually chase either sun or shade depending on the day. Good for beginners and for warming up, and a decent place to bring a couple of pads.
ca_dog_boulder.parking_note: Leave the car in the Horseshoe Lake lot, or at a roadside spot about 200 yards before it.
ca_dog_boulder.approach: Head southeast away from the lake on the forest path; the boulder shows through the trees after a short walk.

ca_onyx_summit_crag.blurb: Onyx Summit Crag is a compact roadside cliff in the San Bernardino Mountains, just off Highway 38 near the Onyx Summit pass above Big Bear, around 8,500 feet. It is mostly a bolted sport crag, with a few easy trad lines and some anchors that make top-roping simple. Routes run from beginner terrain up to the low 5.12s, though most sit in the 5.9 to 5.10 band, and there are a few harder lines for projecting. A pillar with two sharp arete features holds about half the routes, with more on the walls beside it. The sun hits it for much of the day, and the short hike to the base is steeper than it first looks.

ca_north_face_3.blurb: The North Face is the longest sector of Dike Wall, a granite crag on the hillside above Twin Lakes in the Mammoth Lakes basin, at roughly 9,300 feet. As the name says, it faces north, so it stays cool on summer days, though a big snowbank can linger at the base late into the season. Most of the twenty or so climbs are single-pitch sport lines, with a few trad pitches mixed in. Grades start around 5.8 and are concentrated in the 5.10 and 5.11 range, with a handful of 5.12s and low 5.13s. Expect a short but real uphill walk from the lake parking area.
ca_north_face_3.parking_note: Leave the car at the Lake George parking area in the Mammoth Lakes basin.
ca_north_face_3.approach: From the Lake George parking area, walk around the lake to the far shore, then follow a climbers' trail up the slope to the wall.

ca_elephant_knob.blurb: Elephant Knob is a rounded granite dome at about 5,100 feet in the Kern River country near Johnsondale, one of the lowest and easiest-to-reach formations in the Needles area. Nearly all of the roughly twenty routes are trad, typically one to three pitches, with a single aid line. Grades run from the high 5.6s into the low 5.11s, with a fair number of moderates, which makes it a fit for newer leaders. A wildfire years ago peeled flakes from the rock and scorched fixed gear, so check slings and anchors with care and carry your own. A creek below has a swimming hole.
ca_elephant_knob.parking_note: Drive the forest road north of Johnsondale (22S82) to its junction with 22S53 and pull into a small turnout along 22S53.

ca_motherlode_rock_east_face.blurb: Motherlode Rock's eastern side is a long, fairly low slab in the Holcomb Valley Pinnacles, near Big Bear in the San Bernardino Mountains at about 7,500 feet. Roughly twenty routes are spread along it, thickest toward the left end, mostly short sport and trad pitches with a few top-rope lines. Grades range from beginner-level up to the low 5.11s, with plenty in the 5.9 to 5.11 range. The rock is grippy and grainy, with small holds that reward careful footwork. The face catches morning light and goes into shade after midday, and top-rope groups sometimes gather here, so patience helps. Reach it on a short trail from the Pinnacles trail network.

ca_high_bluffs.blurb: High Bluffs (South) is a seaside crag on the far northwest California coast, close to the Humboldt and Del Norte line near Lost Rocks. About twenty routes, mostly sport with some trad and a few top-rope lines, climb pocketed rock with plenty of incut holds. Most grades fall between 5.8 and 5.11, with the largest cluster at the easier end, and the bolts have been fully replaced. Climbs begin on three big boulders or on the beach itself at low tide. It is not a beginner outing: access involves some exposed scrambling, rescue is hard, and winter swells can wash out the base, so check tide and swell first. Ocean breezes keep it cool.

ca_memorial_boulder.blurb: Memorial Boulder is a single glacial erratic sitting in a parking lot in downtown Truckee, formerly known as the Veterans Hall boulder. It is a quick, urban stop rather than a destination: the walk from your car is only a few steps. Around twenty problems cover a very wide range, from a very easy line up to a V11. The front side has the gentler problems, while the back holds the harder, more serious ones. The base is partly paved over, which limits the landings, so pads and spotters matter. It is a handy evening session if you are already in town.

_conflicts.ca_dog_boulder: Stored rock is rhyolite and stored aspect is N, but both pages describe granite with problems on all sides: https://www.mountainproject.com/area/108206864/dog-boulder and https://app.advcollective.com/climbing/dog-boulder-a-granite-playground-for-technique-focused-boulderers
_conflicts.ca_onyx_summit_crag: Stored rock is granodiorite; one page calls it quartz, the other granite: https://openairbigbear.blogspot.com/2011/03/onyx-crag-climbing.html and https://www.mountainproject.com/area/105805245/onyx-summit-crag
